text: Organocatalytic Remote-Controlled Enantioselective 1,10-Additions of In Situ Generated Alkynyl 2,40-Biphenyl Quinone Methides

Tian Liang,<sup>a</sup> Meiwen Liu,<sup>b</sup> Aman Ullah,<sup>c</sup> Zhibin Yue,<sup>a</sup> Yan Xia,<sup>a</sup> Fang Fang, Pengfei Li,<sup>b,</sup>\* Shao-Fei Ni,<sup>c,</sup>\* and Wenjun Li<sup>a,</sup>\*

Abstract: The strategic incorporation of auxiliary groups has recently established α-functionalized alcohols as versatile electrophilic alkylation reagents, enabling remotely controlled conjugate additions. Strikingly, while quinone methide chemistry has been extensively developed, their extended analogues—featuring spatially separated carbonyl and methide units across biphenyl systems—remain unexplored. Building on the prior work with alkynyl 4,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides, an organocatalytic remotely controlled enantioselective 1,10-additions of in situ-generated alkynyl 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides from α-[4-(2- hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols with 3-arylindoles and indole-2-carboxylates is reported, affording a broad scope of enantioenriched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes, respectively. Combined with control experiments, density functional theory calculations elucidate the reaction mechanism, revealing that the dehydration of α-functionalized alcohols to generate 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides constitutes the rate-limiting step, while enantioselectivity arises from the nucleophilic addition of alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides. Notably, beyond proving 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides as competent intermediates, this work breaks new ground by demonstrating their participation in previously unreported stereoselective 1,10-additions.

The strategic design of auxiliary groups has revolutionized α-functionalized alcohol chemistry in recent years, establishing these substrates as versatile platforms for stereoselective electrophilic alkylation and related transformations.<sup>[1]</sup> In this context, phenol and aniline have emerged as particularly practical auxiliary groups, enabling their corresponding α-functionalized alcohols to in situ generate high-value quinone methides (QMs) and aza-QMs, respectively.<sup>[2]</sup> These reactive intermediates serve as versatile platforms for diversity-oriented synthesis.<sup>[3]</sup> In striking contrast to well-developed QM chemistry, organocatalytic stereoselective reactions of their extended analogues—where carbonyl and methide units reside on separate aromatic rings—remain exceptionally rare. This stems from the inherent challenge of exerting stereocontrol over spatially remote reactive centers in these systems.<sup>[4]</sup> To date, only three landmark examples have been reported in this emerging field. In 2023, Sun and coworkers achieved a breakthrough with the first CPA-catalyzed asymmetric 1,6-conjugate addition to in situ-generated 2-naphthoquinone-8-methides (2-Nap-Q-8-Ms) and their aza-analogues (aza-2-Nap-Q-8-Ms), derived from 8-(hydroxyarylmethyl)naphthalen-2-ols/amines for the synthesis of previously less accessible remotely chiral naphthols and naphthylamines (Scheme 1A).<sup>[5]</sup> Simultaneously, we developed the complementary CPA-catalyzed 1,8-addition to (aza)- 2-naphthoquinone-6-methides ((aza)-2-Nap-Q-6-Ms) from 6-(hydroxydiarylmethy l)naphthalen-2-ols/amines (Scheme 1B),<sup>[6]</sup> enabling efficient synthesis of chiral tetraarylmethanes.<sup>[7]</sup> Continually, we further pioneered stereoselective 1,12-additions using alkynyl 4,4 0- biphenyl quinone methides (4,4 0-BQMs) generated from α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols for construction of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes (Scheme 1C).<sup>[8]</sup> Collectively, these advances systematically expand the auxiliary group design from basic phenol/phenylamine to extend naphthol/naphthylamine and biphenyl systems, creating a versatile platform for CPA-catalyzed remote functionalization of α-substituted alcohols. To further explore the chemistry of BQMs,<sup>[9]</sup> and as our going interesting in developing α-functionalized alcohols,<sup>[6,8,10]</sup> we sought to expand the system from alkynyl 4,4 0-BQMs to their 2,4 0-BQM counterparts, focusing on the regiochemical flexibility of QM formation, the impact of altered π-conjugation patterns on reactivity, and new opportunities for stereocontrol in subsequent transformations. Herein, we report a catalytic asymmetric 1,10-addition to in situ-generated alkynyl 2,40-BQMs derived from α-[4- (2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl] propargyl alcohols (Scheme 1D).<sup>[11]</sup> This remotely controlled transformation demonstrates remarkable substratedirected divergence: 1) With 3-arylindoles, the reaction constructs enantioenriched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles via a dehydration/conjugate addition/annulation cascade; 2) Using indole-2-carboxylates, it forges axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes through a stereoselective dehydration/conjugate addition sequence. Notably, this work not only establishes alkynyl 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides (BQMs) as versatile intermediates for organocatalytic asymmetric transformations but also demonstrates their unique capacity to enable remote stereocontrolled 1,10- conjugate additions and divergent synthesis of enantioenriched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles<sup>[10,12]</sup> and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes.<sup>[13]</sup>

We started our investigation with the model reaction of α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohol 1a and 3-phenylindole 2a in dichloromethane at room temperature for 48 h. Preliminary study employing chiral phosphoric acid CPA-1 as catalyst confirmed the formation of product (S)-3aa via dehydration-conjugate additionannulation cascade reaction, albeit with poor enantioselectivity (12% ee, Table 1, entry 1).<sup>[14]</sup> Following systematic evaluation of chiral phosphoric acid catalysts (Table 1, entries 2–8), CPA-2 emerged as the optimal catalyst, delivering product (S)-3aa in 96% yield with 88% ee (Table 1, entry 2). To further enhance enantioselectivity, we investigated solvent effects (Table 1, entries 9–15). Pleasingly, employing $\mathrm { C H C l } _ { 3 }$ as reaction medium in the CPA-2 catalyzed transformation afforded (S)-3aa in 97% yield with 90% ee (Table 1, entry 9). However, lowering the reaction temperature significantly reduced the product yield (Table 1, entry 16), while variations in concentration showed similar results (Table 1, entries 17–18).

With the optimal conditions in hand, we then examined the substrate scope of the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction of propargyl alcohols 1 and 3-arylindoles 2 (Scheme 2). Firstly, the scope ofpropargyl alcohols 1 was investigated by the CPA-2 catalyzed reactions of 3-phenylindole 2a. Generally, all probed propargyl alcohols 1a-j reacted smoothly with 3-arylindole 2 to furnish the desired products (S)-3aa-ja in 91–99% yields with 85–90% ee. Various substituents (R<sup>1</sup>) bearing either electron-withdrawing (F, Cl, Br) or electron-donating groups (Me, MeO) were compatible with a slight effect on reaction efficiency and asymmetric induction. Neither significant electronic nor steric effect of the aromatic moiety was observed. Particularly, the reactions of propargyl alcohols with sterically hindered residue $\overset { \cdot } { ( } R ^ { 1 } \overset { \cdot } { = } 2 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { C l C } _ { 6 } \mathrm { H } _ { 4 } , \ 2 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { M e C } _ { 6 } \mathrm { H } _ { 4 } )$ also proceeded smoothly to afford the corresponding products (S)-3ka in 90% yield with 80% ee and (S)-3la in 98% yield with 76% ee, respectively. Furthermore, the heteroaryl substituted propargyl alcohol 1m was also tolerated to generate the desired product (S)-3ma in 98% yield with 90% ee. Importantly, the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction could be scaled up to 1.25 mmol, affording the product (S)-3aa in 92% yield without compromising the enantioselectivity. The absolute configuration of product (S)-3aa was confirmed by X-ray crystallography (CCDC 2440306). The absolute configurations of other products 3 were assigned by analogy.

text: With these encouraging data in hand, we subsequently investigated the scope of 3-arylindoles 2 by the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction of propargyl alcohol 1a. Notably, a broad scope of 3-arylindoles 2b-l with different substituents $( \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } / \hat { \mathbb { R } } ^ { 3 } )$ reacted smoothly with propargyl alcohol 1a to afford the products (S)-3ab-al in high to excellent yields (77–99%) with high enantioselectivities (80–89% ee). Either electron-withdrawing (F, Cl, Br) or electron-donating groups (Me, MeO) could be introduced into the aromatic ring of 3-arylindoles with a little influence on the yield and ee. Notably, 3-methylindole 2m was also compatible to afford the corresponding product (S)-3am in 97% yield with 80% ee. In all, we developed a class of α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl] propargyl alcohols to react smoothly with 3-arylindoles via dehydration-conjugate addition-annulation cascade reaction, affording a series of 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles in high to excellent yields with high enantioselectivities.

Next, we turned our attention to the chiral phosphoric acid catalyzed asymmetric reactions of α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols 1 with indole-2- carboxylates 4 (Scheme 3). Initial result demonstrated that chiral phosphoric acid CPA-2 failed to promote the desired reaction between propargyl alcohol 1a and indole-2-carboxylate 4a in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C l } _ { 2 }$ Encouragingly, axially chiral tetrasubstituted allene (S)-5aa could be obtained in 97% yield with 86% ee in the presence of CPA-7 in $\mathrm { C H C l } _ { 3 }$ at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h after systematic screening of chiral phosphoric acids and optimization of reaction parameters including solvent, additives, concentration, temperature, and time (see Supporting Information for more details).

Subsequently, we examined the scope of the CPA-7 catalyzed reaction of alcohols 1 and indole-2- carboxylates 4 (Scheme 4). Notably, a broad scope of indole-2-carboxylates bearing $\mathbb { R } ^ { 4 } / \bar { \mathbb { R } } ^ { \bar { 5 } }$ substituents was compatible to afford the desired axially chiral allenes in generally good to high yields and stereoselectivities (Scheme 4A). More specifically, the ester groups of indole-2-carboxylates $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { R } ^ { 4 } )$ had a slight effect on the yield and enantioselectivity, affording the corresponding allenes (S)-5aa-af in 80–97% yields with 70–86% ee, respectively. Regardless of the substituent’s electronic or steric properties, indole-2-carboxylates 4g-k bearing diverse substituents (R<sup>5</sup> = 6-Cl, 6-Br, 5-F, 5-Br, 5-Me) also reacted smoothly with propargyl alcohol 1a to furnish the desired products (S)-5ag-ak in 78–97% yields with 75–93% ee. Exceptionally, racemic product (S)-5al was obtained in 17% yield when 2-phenylindole was employed, suggesting that the substituent at the 2-position significantly influences enantioselectivity. The scope of alcohols 1 was then surveyed by the CPA-7 catalyzed reaction ofindole-2-carboxylate 4a (Scheme 4B). Pleasingly, a series of propargyl alcohols bearing aromatic group with different halogen (F, Cl, Br) were well-tolerated to afford the corresponding axially chiral allenes 5 in 76–95% yields with 77–89% ee. The reaction demonstrated remarkable insensitivity to both electronic and steric variations of the substituents. Moreover, the sterically hindered propargyl alcohol 1p (R<sup>1</sup> = 2-naphthyl) was good substrate to afford the product (S)-5pa in 92% yields with 87% ee. Exceptionally, the aliphatic substituted propargyl alcohol 1q (R<sup>1</sup> = cyclopropanyl) was not compatible. Importantly, the CPA-7 catalyzed reaction of alcohol 1a with indole-2-carboxylate 4a could be scaled up to 1.25 mmol to afford the target product (S)-5aa without compromising reaction efficiency and enantioselectivity (96% yield, 86% ee). The absolute configuration of product 5aa was assigned by comparison between its experimental and calculated electronic circular dichroism (ECD) spectra to be the S configuration (Figure 1).

Taken together, the chiral phosphoric acid catalyzed 1,10-conjugate addition of in situ formed alkynyl 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides from α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols with indole-2-carboxylates, furnishing a wide range of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes in good to high yields and enantioselectivities.

Scheme 4. Substrate scope of reaction between propargyl alcohols 1 and indole-2-carboxylates 4. A mixture of 1 (0.05 mmol), 4 (0.10 mmol), and CPA-7 (2 mol%) in CHCl (0.3 mL) was stirred at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h. Product (S)-5 was obtained in isolated yield. The ee was determined by a chiral-HPLC analysis.

text: To get insight into the reaction mechanism, further investigations were carried out. As shown in Scheme 5A, protection of the hydroxy group in the α-[4-(2- hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohol 1a with a methyl group resulted in dramatically reduced enantioselectivity, affording products (S)-3ra (74% yield, 8% ee) and (S)-5ra (74% yield, 63% ee), respectively. This pronounced erosion of stereocontrol highlights the critical role of the free hydroxyl group in asymmetric induction. Notably, no reaction progression was observed under standard conditions when the nucleophile’s amino group was Boc-protected. This complete lack of reactivity, in stark contrast to the free amine system, unambiguously establishes the indispensable role of the free amino group in both reaction initiation and stereochemical control (Scheme 5B). Control experiment revealed the allene intermediate (Int-allene) could be isolated in 38% yield with 10% ee from the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction of 1a with 2a after 2 h (Scheme 5C). Notably, this intermediate underwent complete conversion to the desired product (S)-3aa under standard conditions, achieving 95% yield and 90% ee. These findings demonstrate that the final product’s optical purity is established during the CPA-2-catalyzed intramolecular annulation of Int-allene, rather than during its initial formation.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations elucidate the CPA-2-catalyzed reaction of 1a with 2a (Figure 2A), revealing a catalytic cycle initiated by hydrogen–bonded complex 2-Int1. Dehydration via 2-TS1 (ΔG<sup>‡</sup> = 26.3 kcal mol-<sup>1</sup>) forms alkynyl 2,40-BQM 2-Int2, then forming a hydrogen–bonded complex 2-Int3 with 2a. Nucleophilic addition of 2a through 2-TS2 vields 2-Int4, which undergoes deprotonation via 2-TS3 to give the thermodynamically stable intermediate 2-Int5. Proton transfer to the allene moiety (2-TS4) forms intermediate 2-Int6 (ΔG = 18.6 kcal mol-<sup>1</sup>), followed by annulation to generate product (S)-3aa. The rate-determining step involves the formation of the $2 { , } 4 ^ { \prime } { \cdot } \mathrm { B Q M }$ intermediate. The enantioselectivity-determining step involves the conversion of 2-Int6 through transition state 2-TS5-S $( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } = 1 6 . 8 \mathrm { k c a l m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$ to furnish the (S)-configured product (S)-3aa while regenerating the CPA-2 catalyst. Comparative analysis of the competing transition states revealed a 4.8 kcal mol-<sup>1</sup> energy difference between the favored 2-TS5-S and its diastereomeric counterpart 2-TS5-R, which correlates well with the experimentally observed 90% enantiomeric excess for the (S)-product (Figure 2B). To quantitatively elucidate the origin of the 4.8 kcal mol-<sup>1</sup> energy difference between 2-TS5-R and 2-TS5-S, we conducted an energy decomposition analysis in the gas phase $( \Delta \Delta E = \mathrm { \ddot { 7 } . 2 \ k c a l \ m o { 1 } ^ { - 1 } ) }$ The results indicate that this energy difference primarily arises from differential distortion energies ofboth the substrate $( \Delta \Delta \mathrm { E _ { s u b } } )$ and the catalyst $( \Delta \Delta \breve { \mathrm { E } } _ { \mathrm { c a t } } )$ . In 2-Int6, the substrate adopts a dihedral angle $( \angle 1 2 3 4 = 4 1 . 8 ^ { \circ } )$ , which undergoes a more significant change in 2-TS5-R $( \angle 1 2 \bar { 3 } 4 = 2 0 . 9 ^ { \circ } )$ than in 2-TS5-S (∠1234 = 34.3°) to facilitate N─C bond formation. Similarly, the catalyst distortion results from a dihedral angle change from $\angle 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 = - 1 1 9 . 3 ^ { \circ }$ in 2-Int6 to $- 1 \bar { 1 } 8 . 3 ^ { \circ }$ in 2-TS5-S and 68.2° in 2-TS5-R. The substantial steric repulsion in 2-TS5-R leads to pronounced structural distortion in both the substrate and catalyst, which exhibits significantly higher distortion energy than 2-TS5-S, indicating that the (R)-pathway requires more extensive structural deformation of both components. These findings strongly support that the observed enantioselectivity stems from the more favorable geometric accommodation of the substrate-catalyst system in the (S)-configured transition state. text: In Figure 3B, energy decomposition analysis attributes this preference to stronger substrate-catalyst interactions in 7-TS2-S, which features an optimized network of five hydrogen bonds (S═O···H: 1.687/2.126/2.280 Å;

P═O···H: 2.066/2.276 Å) versus only three weaker interactions in TS2-R (S═O···H: 1.665/2.507 Å; P═O···H: 1.972 Å), demonstrating how precise non–covalent interaction patterning governs asymmetric induction.

In conclusion, building on our previous success with 4-phenylphenol-based α-functionalized alcohols, we have now demonstrated that 2-phenylphenol serves as an effective auxiliary group for stereodivergent transformations of the corresponding α-functionalized alcohol. In the presence of CPA, alkynyl $2 { , } 4 ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { - } } \mathrm { B Q M s }$ were generated in situ from α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl] propargyl alcohols and subsequently underwent substratecontrolled enantioselective 1,10-conjugate additions, delivering either enantioenriched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles when employing 3-arylindoles as nucleophiles, or axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes when using indole-2-carboxylates. Comprehensive mechanistic studies combining control experiments and DFT calculations not only confirmed the intermediacy of $2 { , } 4 ^ { \prime } { \cdot } \mathrm { B Q M s }$ but also elucidated the reaction pathways. This work represents the first successful implementation oforganocatalytic enantioselective 1,10-additions to 2,4 0-BQMs, establishing a versatile platform for divergent synthesis oftwo privileged chiral scaffolds from common precursors.

General procedure for products (S)-3: To a solution of CHCl (0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.06 mmol), 3-phenylindoles 2 (0.05 mmol), and CPA-2 (0.001 mmol). The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 48 h, and then the solvent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which was purified by silica gel chromatography to yield products (S)-3.

General procedure for products (S)-5: To a solution of CHCl (0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.05 mmol), 2-indole derivatives 4 (0.1 mmol), and CPA-7 (0.001 mmol). The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 24 h, and then the solvent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which was purified by silica gel chromatography to yield products (S)-5.
